title: 06 — Neural Networks and Transformers from Scratch
html:
06 — Neural Networks and Transformers from Scratch

The one idea: a neural network is layers of weighted sums with simple non-linear functions in between, trained by backpropagation, which is the chain rule applied layer by layer. A transformer adds one powerful layer, attention, that lets every token look at every other token. Language models, embedding models and document models are all built from these two ideas.

1. What it is

Concept Meaning
Neuron, layer A weighted sum plus a non-linear activation (tanh, ReLU, GELU). A layer is many neurons in parallel
Forward pass Compute outputs from inputs
Backpropagation Compute the gradient of the loss for every weight, from the output back to the input, using the chain rule
Optimiser Rule for updating weights from gradients: SGD, Adam, AdamW
Embedding A learned vector that represents a token, word, document or entity
Attention Each position computes a weighted mix of all positions' values. Weights come from query-key similarity
Transformer Stacks of attention plus feed-forward layers, with residual connections and normalisation
LLM A large transformer trained to predict the next token, then tuned to follow instructions

2. Why it matters

  • Document AI (layout models, vision-language models), embeddings for search, and LLMs for extraction and classification are all transformers.
  • Knowing what attention computes explains context limits, cost (which grows with sequence length), and why chunking and retrieval matter.
  • Fine-tuning (07) only makes sense once you know what is being trained.

3. The main ideas, beginner to expert

3.1 Beginner: why depth and non-linearity

A single linear layer can only draw straight decision boundaries. Adding a hidden layer with a non-linear activation lets the network bend boundaries. The example below learns an XOR-like pattern (positive when both features have the same sign), which no straight line can separate.

3.2 Intermediate: backpropagation in four lines

For output p, hidden layer h = tanh(XW₁) and log-loss:

  1. d_out = p − y (gradient at the output, for sigmoid with log-loss)
  2. dW₂ = hᵀ · d_out
  3. d_h = (d_out · W₂ᵀ) × (1 − h²) (the chain rule through tanh)
  4. dW₁ = Xᵀ · d_h

Frameworks (PyTorch, JAX) compute these automatically (autograd), but it is the same arithmetic.

3.3 Senior: attention and the transformer block

---
title: One transformer block
---
flowchart TD
    IN["Token embeddings + positions"] --> N1["Layer norm"]
    N1 --> ATT["Multi-head self-attention<br/>softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V"]
    ATT --> R1["+ residual"]
    IN --> R1
    R1 --> N2["Layer norm"]
    N2 --> FF["Feed-forward network<br/>(expand, activation, project)"]
    FF --> R2["+ residual"]
    R1 --> R2
    R2 --> OUT["To next block"]
  • Q = XW_q, K = XW_k, V = XW_v. The scores QKᵀ/√d say how relevant each token is to each other token. Softmax turns each row into weights, and the output is those weights times V.
  • Multi-head: several attention computations in parallel, each free to focus on different relations.
  • Causal mask: in a decoder (GPT-style) model, a token can only attend to earlier tokens, so it can be trained to predict the next one.
  • Cost: attention is quadratic in sequence length, which is why long documents are chunked or processed with efficient attention.
  • Embedding models pool the final vectors into one vector per text. Vision-language models turn image patches into tokens, so attention covers text and layout together.

4. Working code

The script trains a two-layer network with hand-written backpropagation, then computes scaled dot-product attention for a four-token sentence. numpy only.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# 1. A two-layer neural network learns XOR-like data that no straight line can separate.
X = rng.uniform(-1, 1, (400, 2))
y = ((X[:, 0] * X[:, 1]) > 0).astype(float).reshape(-1, 1)     # same sign -> 1
W1, b1 = rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 8)), np.zeros(8)
W2, b2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (8, 1)), np.zeros(1)
sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
for epoch in range(3001):
    h = np.tanh(X @ W1 + b1)                    # forward pass: hidden layer
    p = sigmoid(h @ W2 + b2)                    # forward pass: output probability
    loss = -np.mean(y * np.log(p + 1e-9) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p + 1e-9))
    d_out = (p - y) / len(X)                    # backward pass: gradient at the output
    dW2, db2 = h.T @ d_out, d_out.sum(0)
    d_h = (d_out @ W2.T) * (1 - h ** 2)         # chain rule through tanh
    dW1, db1 = X.T @ d_h, d_h.sum(0)
    for param, grad in ((W1, dW1), (b1, db1), (W2, dW2), (b2, db2)):
        param -= 1.0 * grad                     # gradient descent step, in place
    if epoch in (0, 500, 3000):
        print(f"epoch {epoch:4d}: loss {loss:.3f}, accuracy {((p > 0.5) == y).mean():.2f}")

# 2. Scaled dot-product attention, the core of a transformer, for a 4-token sentence.
tokens = ["NAV", "rose", "after", "split"]
d = 4
E = rng.normal(0, 1, (4, d))                     # token embeddings (normally learned)
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(0, 1, (d, d)) for _ in range(3))
Q, K, V = E @ Wq, E @ Wk, E @ Wv                 # queries, keys, values
scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)                    # how much each token attends to each other token
weights = np.exp(scores - scores.max(1, keepdims=True))
weights /= weights.sum(1, keepdims=True)         # softmax: each row sums to 1
out = weights @ V                                # each token becomes a weighted mix of all values
print("attention weights (row = token attending, columns =", tokens, "):")
for tok, row in zip(tokens, weights):
    print(f"  {tok:6s}", np.round(row, 2))
print("output shape:", out.shape, "- same as the input: one new vector per token")

Output:

epoch    0: loss 0.944, accuracy 0.48
epoch  500: loss 0.068, accuracy 0.98
epoch 3000: loss 0.033, accuracy 0.99
attention weights (row = token attending, columns = ['NAV', 'rose', 'after', 'split'] ):
  NAV    [0.17 0.35 0.18 0.29]
  rose   [0.08 0.43 0.22 0.27]
  after  [0.83 0.02 0.08 0.08]
  split  [0.27 0.23 0.18 0.33]
output shape: (4, 4) - same as the input: one new vector per token

What to notice:

  • Loss falls from 0.944 to 0.033, and accuracy reaches 0.99, on a pattern a linear model can't learn. (This is training accuracy. A real project would also check a held-out set.)
  • Each attention row sums to 1. Each token's output is a weighted mix of all tokens' value vectors. The weights here come from random projections. In a trained model they encode useful relations, such as "split" attending to "NAV".
  • The output has one vector per token, the same shape as the input. That is why blocks can be stacked.

The same layer in PyTorch (not run: PyTorch wasn't installed in the build environment):

# Not run.
import torch, torch.nn as nn
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 8), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(8, 1))
optimiser = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
for epoch in range(2000):
    optimiser.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(X_t), y_t)
    loss.backward()            # autograd does the chain rule
    optimiser.step()

5. Common mistakes

  1. Unscaled inputs. Training becomes slow or unstable.
  2. Learning rate too high or too low. Watch the loss curve.
  3. Evaluating on training data only. Always hold data out.
  4. Treating attention weights as explanations. They hint at relations but are not faithful explanations.
  5. Ignoring sequence length. Cost and memory grow fast with it.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. Replace tanh with ReLU (max(0, z), derivative z > 0) and compare convergence.
  2. Add a held-out set and report validation accuracy.
  3. Add a causal mask to the attention example (set future positions' scores to −∞ before softmax) and check that each row only weights earlier tokens.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why does a network need a non-linear activation?
  2. What does backpropagation compute?
  3. Write the attention formula.
  4. What does a causal mask do?
  5. Why is attention expensive for long documents?

Answers

  1. Without one, stacked linear layers collapse into a single linear function.
  2. The gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, via the chain rule.
  3. softmax(QKᵀ / √d) · V.
  4. It stops a token attending to later tokens, so the model can be trained for next-token prediction.
  5. Every token attends to every other token, so cost grows with the square of the length.

8. Sources
